title: Linear Recurrences and Rational Generating Functions

items.title: Constant-coefficient linear recurrences, their starting index and their characteristic polynomial
Rational formal power series, proper presentations and reduced denominators
The initial-value, recurrence-sequence, numerator and fixed-denominator rational-series spaces all have dimension $d$
items.strategy: For $Q(x)=1+c_1x+\cdots+c_dx^d$ with $c_d\ne0$, use coefficient extraction to identify a recurrence sequence with its first $d$ values and with the degree-$<d$ polynomial $QF$. Division by the unit $Q$ identifies that numerator space with the proper series $P/Q$. The four maps are linear inverse pairs, and the standard basis of $K^d$ supplies the dimension count.

items.title: A coefficient sequence is eventually linearly recurrent if and only if its formal generating function is rational
items.strategy: Use the four-space lemma for a recurrence valid from index zero. For a later starting index, subtract the finite exceptional prefix; conversely polynomial division separates any rational series into a polynomial prefix and a proper fixed-denominator part. State the sharper fixed-$Q$ clause: the recurrence starts at zero exactly when $QF$ has degree below $\deg Q$.

items.title: $d$ initial values determine a sequence satisfying a fixed order-$d$ recurrence
items.strategy: Apply the initial-value isomorphism in the four-space lemma. Include $d=1$ explicitly and note that order zero is reserved for the eventually zero case rather than folded into this statement.

items.title: The least eventual recurrence order is the degree of the reduced denominator
items.strategy: Normalize the reduced rational presentation by $Q(0)=1$. The equivalence theorem turns every order-$e$ recurrence into a denominator of degree $e$; coprimeness forces the reduced denominator to divide it. The displayed reduced denominator itself supplies a recurrence of its own degree, with the polynomial-series case giving order zero.

items.title: Changing finitely many coefficients preserves rationality and eventual linear recurrence
items.strategy: The difference of the two generating functions is a polynomial. Rational series are closed under adding a polynomial, and the equivalence theorem converts this statement back to eventual recurrences. Record that a finite change can destroy a recurrence beginning at index zero.

items.title: For a bi-infinite linear recurrence over $K$, the two half-series satisfy $F_+(x)=-F_-(x^{-1})$ in $K(x)$
items.strategy: Let $K$ be a field and use the nonzero trailing recurrence coefficient to propagate the sequence in both directions. The recurrence-rational equivalence puts both half-series in the rational function field $K(x)$. Multiply the positive and reversed-negative series by reciprocal denominators and compare their finite boundary numerators there, obtaining $F_+(x)=-F_-(x^{-1})$ as an equality of rational functions, not formal power series. Absorb the resulting degree-gap and endpoint-coefficient symmetry into the final clause.

items.title: Rational formal power series are closed under sums and Cauchy products
items.strategy: Put two presentations over the common denominator $Q_1Q_2$. Its constant coefficient is a unit, so both the sum numerator $P_1Q_2+P_2Q_1$ and the product numerator $P_1P_2$ define rational formal series. Include zero and polynomial denominators.

items.title: The Hadamard product of two rational formal power series over a field is rational
items.strategy: Translate rationality to eventual recurrences and discard finite prefixes. The shifts of each recurrent sequence lie in a finite span; products of one shift from each sequence span every simultaneous shift of the coefficientwise product. A linear dependence among sufficiently many shifts gives an eventual recurrence, and the equivalence theorem returns rationality.

items.title: Reciprocal-root convention: $\chi(t)=\prod_i(t-\lambda_i)^{m_i}$ corresponds to $Q(x)=\prod_i(1-\lambda_i x)^{m_i}$
A proper rational function with split denominator has a unique repeated-pole partial-fraction expansion
items.strategy: For pairwise distinct nonzero $\lambda_i$, the powers $(1-\lambda_i x)^{m_i}$ are pairwise coprime. Repeated Bezout decomposition gives existence of $\sum_{i,j}b_{ij}(1-\lambda_i x)^{-j}$; clearing denominators and reducing modulo each prime-power factor gives uniqueness.

items.title: Repeated poles expand formally as $(1-\lambda x)^{-j}=\sum_{n\ge0}\binom{n+j-1}{j-1}\lambda^n x^n$
items.strategy: Induct on $j$. The base case is the formal geometric series; multiplying by $(1-\lambda x)^{-1}$ and applying the hockey-stick identity, obtained by a short induction from Pascal's rule, to the Cauchy convolution gives the next exponent. No analytic convergence is invoked.

items.title: Over a named splitting field in characteristic zero, repeated characteristic roots give polynomial-times-exponential closed forms
items.strategy: Let $E/K$ be a splitting field of the recurrence characteristic polynomial and write $\chi(t)=\prod_i(t-\lambda_i)^{m_i}$. Use the reciprocal-root convention, the split partial fractions lemma and the repeated-pole binomial expansion. In characteristic zero the factorial scalar is nonzero and invertible, so the published falling-factorial formula makes each binomial coefficient a polynomial in $n$; hence $a_n=\sum_i p_i(n)\lambda_i^n$ with $\deg p_i<m_i$. Prove uniqueness from uniqueness of partial fractions, and state equality in $E$ rather than silently assuming $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$.

items.title: The row-shift companion matrix of a linear recurrence
The companion matrix advances the recurrence state vector by one step
items.strategy: Multiply the companion matrix by $(a_n,\ldots,a_{n+d-1})^{\mathsf T}$. The shift rows copy the last $d-1$ coordinates and the final row is exactly the recurrence; induction then gives the state vector at time $n$ as the $n$th matrix power applied to the initial state.

items.title: A recurrence companion matrix has the recurrence characteristic polynomial
items.strategy: Compute $\det(tI-C)$ by Laplace expansion along the first column, or equivalently induct on the size of its Hessenberg form. The signs leave $t^d+c_1t^{d-1}+\cdots+c_d$, including the $d=1$ case.

items.title: For an invertible matrix over a field, Cayley–Hamilton makes every matrix-power entry and trace sequence linearly recurrent
items.strategy: Let $K$ be a field, let $n\ge1$, and take an invertible matrix $A\in M_n(K)$. Apply Cayley–Hamilton to the coordinate endomorphism represented by $A$, multiply the resulting matrix identity by successive powers of $A$, and extract an entry or take trace. The constant term of $\chi_A$ is $(-1)^n\det(A)$, which is nonzero because an invertible matrix has unit determinant; hence the resulting order-$n$ relation has the nonzero trailing coefficient required by the page's recurrence definition.

items.title: The Fibonacci sequence $F_0=0,F_1=1$ and Lucas sequence $L_0=2,L_1=1$
The trace of a square matrix over a commutative ring
For matrices over a field, the commutative-ring trace agrees with the published matrix trace
items.strategy: Both definitions are the same finite sum of the diagonal entries with the same zero-size empty-sum convention. Unfold the two definitions and compare term by term.

items.title: Finite weighted directed multigraphs, weighted walks and their transfer matrices
The $(u,v)$ entry of $A^n$ is the total weight of length-$n$ walks from $u$ to $v$
items.strategy: Induct on $n$. At $n=0$, the identity matrix records the unique empty walk when $u=v$ and none otherwise. For the induction step, partition walks by their penultimate vertex and last edge; matrix multiplication performs exactly the resulting finite sum of products.

items.title: Formally, $(I-xA)^{-1}=\sum_{n\ge0}A^n x^n$ over every commutative coefficient ring
items.strategy: Define the matrix series coefficientwise in $M_p(R\llbracket x\rrbracket)$. Multiplication by $I-xA$ telescopes coefficient by coefficient on both sides, with constant coefficient $I$ and every positive coefficient zero. This is a formal identity and uses no norm, spectral radius or convergence hypothesis.

items.title: Transfer-matrix theorem: weighted-walk generating functions are cofactors of $I-xA$ divided by $\det(I-xA)$
items.strategy: For a nonempty $p$-vertex weighted digraph, the formal matrix geometric lemma makes $M=I-xA$ invertible. Its determinant has constant coefficient $1$, hence is a unit. Apply the published adjugate inverse formula over $R\llbracket x\rrbracket$ and read the $(u,v)$ entry as $(-1)^{u+v}\det(M^{(v,u)})/\det(M)$. The weighted-walk theorem identifies that entry with the desired generating series.

items.title: $\frac{d}{dx}\det(I-xA)=-\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}(I-xA)A)$
items.strategy: Differentiate the permutation expansion of the determinant using the formal product rule. Group terms by the differentiated matrix entry; the coefficient is its cofactor. Since $(I-xA)'=-A$, the sum is the negative trace of $\operatorname{adj}(I-xA)A$. The proof is valid over an arbitrary commutative ring.

items.title: Closed walks have trace and logarithmic-derivative generating functions
items.strategy: Sum the diagonal entries in the transfer-matrix identity to get $\sum_{n\ge0}\operatorname{tr}(A^n)x^n=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}(I-xA))/Q(x)$. For positive lengths, multiply the derivative lemma by $-x/Q(x)$ and use the formal inverse series to obtain $\sum_{n\ge1}\operatorname{tr}(A^n)x^n=-xQ'(x)/Q(x)$, where $Q=\det(I-xA)$.

items.title: Let $K$ be a field, $p\ge1$, and $A\in M_p(K)$. If $\chi_A(t)=\prod_{i<p}(t-\lambda_i)$ in $K[t]$, then the transfer-matrix trace series is $\sum_{i<p}(1-\lambda_i x)^{-1}$
items.strategy: Assume the displayed factorisation of $\chi_A$. It is exactly the hypothesis required by spectral mapping and the trace theorem. Applying spectral mapping to $t^n$ and then the trace theorem gives $\operatorname{tr}(A^n)=\sum_{i<p}\lambda_i^n$. Sum the formal geometric series to obtain $\sum_{n\ge0}\operatorname{tr}(A^n)x^n=\sum_{i<p}(1-\lambda_i x)^{-1}$.

items.title: Finite words, contiguous factors, avoidance and proper-prefix states
The longest-suffix prefix automaton for a finite set of forbidden factors
Words over a finite alphabet avoiding finitely many nonempty factors have a rational length generating function
items.strategy: Prove that after an allowed letter is appended, the longest suffix that is a proper prefix of a forbidden factor is a sufficient state, while a completed forbidden factor is rejected. Thus accepted words of length $n$ are walks of length $n$ in the finite prefix automaton from the empty state to any allowed state. Sum the relevant transfer-matrix entries and invoke the cofactor formula.

items.title: Binary words avoiding any fixed nonempty factor have a rational length generating function
items.strategy: Specialize the finite-forbidden-set theorem to alphabet $\{0,1\}$ and the singleton forbidden set $\{w\}$. The nonempty hypothesis prevents the empty word from being forbidden and leaves a nonempty start state.

title: Examples: Linear Recurrences and Rational Generating Functions

items.title: The Fibonacci generating function and Binet formula over $\mathbb Q(\sqrt5)$
items.strategy: Multiply $F(x)=\sum F_nx^n$ by $1-x-x^2$ to get $x$. Name $\mathbb Q(\sqrt5)$ as a splitting field of $t^2-t-1$, use the reciprocal-root convention and solve the two initial-value equations for the coefficients. No growth or limiting claim is made.

items.title: The Lucas generating function and its two-root closed form
items.strategy: Use $L_0=2,L_1=1$ with the same recurrence to obtain $(2-x)/(1-x-x^2)$. In $\mathbb Q(\sqrt5)$ the initial conditions give $L_n=\phi^n+\widehat\phi^n$, displaying the same characteristic roots with different coefficients from Fibonacci.

items.title: The repeated pole $(1-2x)^{-2}$ produces the sequence $(n+1)2^n$
items.strategy: Apply the repeated-pole binomial series at $j=2$ and $\lambda=2$. Verify directly that the characteristic polynomial is $(t-2)^2$ and that the polynomial factor has degree one, exactly one below the root multiplicity.

items.title: The Fibonacci companion matrix advances $(F_n,F_{n+1})$
items.strategy: For $t^2-t-1$, write $C=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ and verify $(F_{n+1},F_{n+2})^{\mathsf T}=C(F_n,F_{n+1})^{\mathsf T}$. Induction gives the standard matrix-power identity and the companion characteristic-polynomial theorem gives $t^2-t-1$.

items.title: Monomer–domino tilings of a board give the Fibonacci recurrence and transfer matrix
items.strategy: Partition tilings of length $n$ by their last tile to obtain $T_n=T_{n-1}+T_{n-2}$ with $T_0=T_1=1$, hence $T_n=F_{n+1}$. Encode the two boundary states by the Fibonacci transfer matrix and use the walk theorem to recover $1/(1-x-x^2)$ formally.

items.title: Cyclic monomer–domino tilings are counted by Lucas numbers through a matrix trace
items.strategy: Use closed walks in the two-state Fibonacci transfer graph to encode tilings with the initial and terminal boundary matched. Compute $\operatorname{tr}(C^n)=L_n$ from the shared recurrence and the values at $n=1,2$, and obtain the generating function from the trace form. State the small circular-board convention explicitly.

items.title: Closed walks of length $n$ in $K_p$ are counted by $(p-1)^n+(p-1)(-1)^n$
items.strategy: Let $p,n\ge1$ and work over $\mathbb Q$. For the adjacency matrix $A=J-I$ of $K_p$, the all-ones vector and the vectors $e_i-e_0$ for $1\le i<p$ give a basis in which $A$ is diagonal with entries $p-1,-1,\ldots,-1$. Hence $\chi_A(t)=(t-(p-1))(t+1)^{p-1}$ is a product of linear factors over $\mathbb Q$. Apply the transfer-matrix trace formula to obtain $\operatorname{tr}(A^n)=(p-1)^n+(p-1)(-1)^n$, which is the number of closed walks of length $n$. For $p=1$, the list $e_i-e_0$ is empty and the same calculation gives zero.

items.title: Binary words avoiding $11$ are counted by $F_{n+2}$
items.strategy: Use prefix states $\varepsilon$ and $1$. Their transfer matrix is the Fibonacci matrix up to state order; summing walks from the empty state gives counts $1,2,3,5,\ldots$ and generating function $(1+x)/(1-x-x^2)$.

items.title: Binary words avoiding $101$ have generating function $(1+x^2)/(1-2x+x^2-x^3)$
items.strategy: Use the proper-prefix states $\varepsilon,1,10$, write the $3\times3$ transition matrix, and sum its walks from $\varepsilon$ to all allowed states. The first counts $1,2,4,7,12,21,37$ verify the numerator and denominator through length six.

items.title: North–east–west walks without immediate horizontal reversal satisfy $a_n=2a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}$
items.strategy: Classify a walk by its last step and forbid $EW$ and $WE$. Eliminate the three state counts to obtain the stated recurrence, then derive the rational generating function both from that recurrence and from the $3\times3$ transfer matrix as a consistency check.

items.title: A recurrence over $\mathbb Q$ can require a proper splitting field for its exponential closed form
items.strategy: Take $a_{n+2}+a_n=0$ with $a_0=0,a_1=1$. Its generating function $x/(1+x^2)$ is rational over $\mathbb Q$, but its characteristic polynomial $t^2+1$ has no root there and splits over $\mathbb Q(i)$. Give the resulting closed form in that named field.

items.title: The recurrence coefficients alone determine the sequence
items.strategy: Refute the claim using two different initial pairs for $a_{n+2}=a_{n+1}+a_n$, for example $(0,0)$ and $(0,1)$. The initial-value corollary explains precisely what extra data are missing.

items.title: A split characteristic polynomial always gives a linear combination of pure exponentials
items.strategy: Refute the claim by $a_n=n$, whose characteristic polynomial $(t-1)^2$ is split but whose closed form needs the degree-one factor $n$. Relate the obstruction to the repeated-pole example and the multiplicity bound in the closed-form theorem.

items.title: $\sum_{n\ge0}n!x^n$ is a formal power series that is not rational over $\mathbb Q$
items.strategy: If $n!$ obeyed an eventual constant-coefficient recurrence, divide the relation at index $n$ by $n!$. The result is a monic polynomial identity in $n$ with infinitely many roots, contradicting the root bound obtained from polynomial division. Invoke the recurrence–rational equivalence; use no convergence or growth argument.

items.title: The transfer-matrix identity requires a spectral-radius or convergence hypothesis
items.strategy: Refute the assertion by the coefficientwise telescoping proof of $(I-xA)^{-1}=\sum A^nx^n$ in $M_p(R\llbracket x\rrbracket)$. Point out that the constant coefficient $I$ supplies formal invertibility over every commutative ring, independently of any topology.
